about: Data of Learn lesson A5, Will there be enough power when it matters? The Plains Grid, its fleet, its outage rates and every resource added are fictional and illustrative. Demand, wind and sun follow the real hourly shapes of the Southwest Power Pool grid in 2025 (town_year.json) and 2024 (m03-capacity-expansion-2024.json), both from EIA-930, scaled as stated below. The 500 simulated years are resampled: each week of a simulated year is a real week of 2024 or 2025, shifted by at most one week; they are not 500 observed weather years. The reference block holds the simulation's results at seed 2025.

grid.name: Plains Grid
grid.note: Illustrative: a grid planned for a 4,000 MW peak, with a gas and coal fleet, wind and solar, set so that it misses the 1-in-10 criterion before anything is added. Not a model of any real grid.

unitsNote: Forced outage rates and repair times are illustrative. Each unit is either available or out; an outage starts at random and lasts a random number of hours with the stated average, independently of every other unit and of the weather. Planned maintenance is left out.

options.label: Gas peakers
options.detail: 5 units of 100 MW, each out 7% of the time

options.label: Wind farm
options.detail: 500 MW, the same shape as the grid's wind

options.label: Solar farm
options.detail: 500 MW, the same shape as the grid's solar

options.label: 4-hour battery
options.detail: 500 MW, 2,000 MWh, [[round-trip-efficiency|85% round-trip efficiency]] (it returns 85% of the energy that charged it)

options.label: Demand response
options.detail: 500 MW of load that can be cut, at most 4 hours a day

sim.dispatch: Each hour: wind, sun and the available units first; a battery discharges only in a shortfall and charges from any surplus, starting each year full; demand response is called in the first shortfall hours of a day, up to 4 hours a day; anything left is unserved.

criterion.label: 1 day in 10 years
criterion.source: PJM Manual 20A: Resource Adequacy Analysis, Rev. 3, effective 24 June 2026, section 1.3 (p. 8)

pjm.about: PJM's ELCC class ratings for its 2028/2029 Base Residual Auction: the share of each class's capacity PJM counts toward adequacy in that one auction, not universal technology values. PJM's model simulates forced outages as a function of weather (Manual 20A, section 2.3) and rates classes by expected unserved energy (sections 2.4 and 2.6).
pjm.source: PJM, ELCC Class Ratings for the 2028/2029 Base Residual Auction

texts.about: Notes and feedback the page shows (step 2's interval and seed, step 4's screen, a rating at a zero target, step 8's question), each with the model's own numbers.
texts.ZERO_NOTE: No shortfall is left in the 500 years, so the rating is the smallest perfect MW that also leaves none: a limit of the sample, not proof of zero risk.
texts.SE_NOTE: ± two [[standard-error|standard errors]] of the average over 500 years ([[monte-carlo-error|Monte Carlo error]]), given these inputs. It leaves out uncertainty in the weather history and the model's assumptions.
texts.SEED_NOTE: The [[random-seed|seed]] numbers the random draws so a run can be repeated; another seed draws other years with the same assumptions.
texts.RULES_NOTE: Simple operating rules, not optimized: the battery starts each year full, charges from any surplus and discharges only in a shortfall; demand response covers a day's first 4 shortfall hours. Better timing could rate both higher.
texts.SCREEN_NOTE: A deliberately crude screen: every MW counts at nameplate, and 500 MW of demand response counts as 500 MW of supply against the gross 4,000 MW peak.
texts.PJM_SAW: A rating belongs to one grid, one mix and one model. **Correlated outages, such as a cold snap knocking out many units at once, can lower a peaker's rating; Analyst lesson [[lesson:a09-hazards|A9]] brings such hazards in.**

PJM_Q.weather: Yes: PJM simulates outages as a function of weather (Manual 20A, section 2.3); here they are independent. It is one possible contributor; the grids, mixes and formulas differ too.
PJM_Q.metric: No: both rate by expected unserved energy (Manual 20A, sections 2.4 and 2.6), though PJM's formula is a ratio of EUE improvements and this lesson matches perfect MW. The weather assumption differs.
PJM_Q.same: No: PJM ties outages to the weather and this lesson draws them independently; the grids, mixes and formulas differ too.

reference.about: Results of the lesson's simulation of 500 resampled years at seed 2025: the grid as it is, each resource added alone, three blocks of solar and the solar-battery mix; repeats counts, over seeds 1 to 20, the runs in which solar counts for more with the battery than alone, and the battery with solar.
